title: Xi, Putin, Modi and Pezeshkian Converge in Bishkek as SCO Summit Becomes a Counterweight to Washington
subhead: The leaders of China, Russia, India and Iran met at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, where Modi publicly pressed Putin to end the Ukraine war and the bloc framed itself as a counter to US influence. Separately, the US-Iran conflict flared again after a monthlong lull, and Washington's decision to bring Russia back into G20 finance talks angered Europe.

sections.heading: Bishkek Summit Brings the Non-Western Bloc Together
sections.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian gathered in Bishkek for the 25th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, a meeting that AP framed as heads of state 'countering US influence.' Putin and Xi reaffirmed their strategic partnership in talks described by Al Jazeera as taking place amid an 'unpredictable' world, with the two leaders vowing to strengthen bilateral ties.

The most striking moment came in the Modi-Putin bilateral, where the Indian prime minister publicly urged the Russian president to end the war in Ukraine 'for humanity's sake,' according to Reuters. Modi's appeal, delivered as Washington weighs tariffs on Russian oil, underscores India's delicate balancing act between its deepening ties with Moscow and its Western relationships. The New York Times noted the summit showed the 'leverage wars' that the conflict has given Xi, who now sits at the center of a bloc spanning Russia, India and Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: The simultaneous presence of China, Russia, India and Iran — four powers with divergent interests but a shared friction with Washington — signals a consolidating non-Western alignment. Modi's public pressure on Putin shows even Moscow's closest partners are uncomfortable with the war's duration.

sections.heading: US-Iran Conflict Flares Again After a Monthlong Lull
sections.body:
The US struck Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a roughly monthlong pause in direct military exchanges, and Iran retaliated with missile fire at US forces in Jordan, according to the Washington Post, CNN and DW. Trump vowed to hit Iran 'hard' while also suggesting the fighting would likely remain limited, per the Washington Post and NBC News. The UAE separately said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its territorial waters, AP reported.

Despite the flare-up, EnergyNow reported that Washington and Tehran are weighing extending their ceasefire by two weeks, and oil markets swung sharply — prices rose after the strikes before retreating as Trump backed down and agreed to the extension, with Brent falling. The Guardian described the exchange as a 'new flare-up' after the lull, and France 24 said the renewed clashes brought the conflict's lull to an end.
sections.whyItMatters: The strikes confirm the Iran war remains unresolved and volatile, with Hormuz shipping and global energy prices hostage to each escalation. The simultaneous ceasefire-extension talks show both sides still prefer managed escalation over all-out war — but the pattern of periodic flare-ups keeps the world's key energy chokepoint in permanent crisis mode.

sections.heading: China Warns Taiwan Over Pacific Islands Forum Presence
sections.body:
China warned Pacific nations of 'consequences' over Taiwan's attendance at the Pacific Islands Forum meeting in Palau, Reuters and the Japan Times reported. Beijing's warning drew a sharp response from Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who pushed back on the threat, and from Pacific leaders who insisted they determine their own agenda, per SBS and the Australian Financial Review.

The Diplomat noted how great-power rivalry is fracturing the Pacific Islands Forum, with at least five leaders skipping the summit, according to the Taipei Times. AP reported the gathering of some of the world's smallest island nations is being overshadowed by the US-China competition for influence in the region.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pacific Islands Forum has become a frontline of US-China competition, and Beijing's willingness to threaten 'consequences' over Taiwan's participation shows it treats even symbolic diplomatic presence as a red line. The pushback from Australia and Pacific states indicates the region is resisting being drawn into the rivalry.

sections.heading: US Brings Russia Back Into G20 Finance Talks, Angering Europe
sections.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at the G20 finance ministers' gathering, and the US invited Siluanov back to the talks — a move that drew sharp objections from European officials, according to Bloomberg, Politico, the Washington Post and the New York Times. Reuters reported that Bessent told the Russian minister there would be no economic relief until the Ukraine war ends.

The Guardian's Ukraine war briefing quoted Bessent saying pressure would stay on the Russian economy until the war is over. The decision to welcome Russia back to the G20 finance track, after its suspension following the 2022 invasion, marks a significant US policy shift that has isolated Washington from its European allies on the issue.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington's unilateral decision to reintegrate Russia into G20 economic diplomacy — while simultaneously vowing no sanctions relief — reflects a transactional approach that is straining the transatlantic consensus. It also gives Moscow a platform to project normalcy even as the war grinds on.

sections.heading: Army Secretary Driscoll Resigns Amid Friction With Hegseth
sections.body:
US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll submitted his resignation after months of reported friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to the Wall Street Journal, Politico, Axios and the New York Times. The resignation comes as the US military grapples with two simultaneous wars — the Iran conflict and support for Ukraine — and follows a period of turbulence in Pentagon leadership.

The Atlantic described Driscoll's departure as a 'parting shot,' and the Guardian reported the resignation was over friction with Hegseth. The timing, with the US engaged in active operations against Iran and managing a global force posture, raises questions about continuity in Army leadership at a critical moment.
sections.whyItMatters: A service secretary resigning mid-conflict over friction with the defense secretary signals dysfunction at the top of the US military establishment. With the Army central to both the Iran war and European deterrence, leadership instability carries operational risk.

sections.heading: Russia Intensifies 'Gray Zone' Attacks Across Europe
sections.body:
The Wall Street Journal reported that Russia is bombarding Europe with a new wave of 'gray zone' attacks — sabotage, cyberattacks and covert operations — as part of an intensified campaign against Ukraine's allies. Euronews noted the Baltics are pushing back against new fears of a Russian attack, and Euromaidan Press reported Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening even as NATO sees no conventional attack coming.

The campaign comes alongside the CIA director's recent secret visit to Moscow, which El País described as shrouded in 'half-truths' amid a war of Russian espionage in Europe. Trump, meanwhile, said Putin will not attack NATO territory and downplayed the significance of the Ratcliffe trip, per DD News.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's shift toward sabotage and covert operations below the conventional-war threshold is a deliberate strategy to pressure European publics and governments without triggering NATO's Article 5. The widening gray-zone campaign is testing alliance cohesion and resilience in ways that conventional deterrence does not address.

bottomLine: The day's defining development is the convergence of China, Russia, India and Iran in Bishkek — a visible consolidation of the non-Western bloc, with Modi publicly pressing Putin to end the Ukraine war even as the SCO frames itself against US influence. Beneath that, the US-Iran conflict flared again after a monthlong lull before both sides moved toward extending a ceasefire, keeping Hormuz and global energy in a state of managed crisis. Washington's decision to bring Russia back into G20 finance talks, over European objections, and the resignation of Army Secretary Driscoll amid friction with Hegseth, both point to a US foreign policy that is increasingly unilateral and internally strained. The strategic picture is one of hardening bloc lines and a US that is simultaneously escalating, negotiating and reorganizing its own leadership.
